claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its simple solid-solution state.
The low hardness and strength arise because the solid solution lacks effective dislocation barriers.
Nanoscale precipitates and short-range ordering would provide effective dislocation barriers in this alloy.
The as-processed alloy has a uniform lattice with low or mechanically ineffective lattice distortion.
Low lattice distortion and the absence of internal obstacles permit relatively free dislocation glide.
Relatively free dislocation glide explains the favorable plasticity and machinability of CoCrFeNiTi.
The initial material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The initial material is a single-phase, disordered solid solution.
A secondary heat treatment can induce nanoscale precipitates or short-range order in near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
A slight compositional modification can promote ordering without compromising the single-phase state.
The proposed controlled comparison uses identical room-temperature mechanical tests on the initial and modified materials.
Nanoscale precipitates or short-range-ordered domains would act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Minimal dislocation pinning in the initial solid solution causes lower work hardening and strength.
Induced precipitates would strengthen the alloy through an Orowan-type mechanism.
Ordered domains would strengthen the alloy through order strengthening.
Producing precipitates or ordering should measurably increase hardness relative to the starting state.
Producing precipitates or ordering should measurably increase yield strength relative to the starting state.
Reduced dislocation mobility should be evidenced by higher work-hardening rates.
The mechanism applies near room temperature or at similarly low homologous temperatures, provided complex multiphase reactions do not dominate.
Failure to increase hardness and yield strength after verified formation of precipitates or ordered domains would falsify the proposed mechanism.
